lesson.title: Straight Lines and Curves: What a Concentration-Time Plot Really Shows
lesson.summary: Examines the raw, untransformed shape of a concentration-time plot for each reaction order and explains, physically, why first and second order curves bend the way they do.
lesson.body:
The previous section jumped straight to transformed plots like ln[A] versus t. It is worth stepping back and looking at the plain, untransformed [A] versus t curve on its own, because its shape carries real physical meaning, and understanding why it bends the way it does is what makes the transformation trick in the previous section feel like more than just an algebra shortcut.

Start with the simplest case: a zero order reaction, where the differential rate law is rate = k, a constant that does not depend on [A] at all. Because the rate never changes, [A] versus t is a straight line with slope -k, and the reaction has an unusual property that first and second order reactions do not share: it can run out of reactant entirely, at one specific, predictable moment. Worked example: [A]0 = 0.800 M, k = 0.0400 M/min.

[A](15 min) = 0.800 - (0.0400)(15) = 0.800 - 0.600 = 0.200 M
[A](20 min) = 0.800 - (0.0400)(20) = 0.800 - 0.800 = 0.000 M

At t = 20.0 min, the reactant is exactly, completely consumed, a genuine finish line. That is only possible because a straight line eventually crosses zero and, physically, concentration cannot go negative, so the reaction simply stops there.

Now contrast that with the first order data from the previous section's table: 0.500, 0.250, 0.125, 0.0625 M at t = 0, 30, 60, 90 min. From 0.500 M to 0.250 M is a drop of 0.250 M over 30 minutes. From 0.125 M to 0.0625 M is a drop of only 0.0625 M, a much smaller absolute amount, over the exact same 30-minute window. That shrinking drop, even though the time interval never changes, is the defining visual signature of exponential decay, and it happens because the rate itself, rate = k[A], is shrinking right along with the concentration. As [A] gets smaller, the reaction slows down, so it removes less and less material in each successive time interval. Mathematically, this curve keeps approaching zero but never actually reaches it, unlike the zero order line above, which reaches zero cleanly and stops.

Second order curves share that same never-quite-reaches-zero shape as first order, but they fall away from the starting concentration even more steeply at first and then flatten out even more gradually later, a direct visual consequence of the ever-lengthening half-life discussed in the previous two sections. This is exactly why the raw [A] versus t plot, while easy to obtain from data, is a poor tool for telling first and second order reactions apart just by eye. Both produce a curve that looks roughly "fast then slow." Only the algebraic transformations from the previous section, plotting ln[A] or 1/[A] instead of [A] itself, turn that ambiguous curve into an unambiguous straight line, which is exactly the technique formalized next.
